principles.title: How films are chosen
principles.lead: The standard films are judged by, what counts as a Catholic film, and what each profile looks at.

sections.heading: The standard
sections.text:
The Second Vatican Council and the reforms that followed it are not accepted here. Films are judged by Catholic doctrine and moral teaching as the Church taught them before the Council.

That is a standard, not a cut-off date. A film made in 2004 can meet it, and a film made in 1950 can fail it. Three rules follow from it:

items.text: A film is not included if its subject has no title of saint or blessed from before the Council and has been declared one only by the post-conciliar popes. Those declarations are not accepted as canonisations or beatifications, so such a person is not called saint or blessed here. That is no judgment on the person, only on the declaration.

A film is not included if its Catholic content is the post-conciliar Church presented as normal or exemplary: the new liturgy, religious life as reformed after the Council, or interreligious dialogue.

A film about an apparition is included only if the Church approved the apparition before the Council, as with Guadalupe, Lourdes, La Salette or Fátima. Films about apparitions claimed since then, or never approved, such as Medjugorje or Garabandal, are not included.

sections.heading: What counts as a Catholic film
sections.text:
The Catholic faith has to be central to the film: the Mass and the sacraments, the life of a saint, a priest's or a nun's vocation, Our Lady and her apparitions, or a persecution of the Church. A sympathetic priest in a supporting role, a church wedding or a vaguely spiritual mood is not enough.

That leaves out some well-loved films that simply have Catholic characters in them.

sections.heading: What each film is judged on
sections.text: Every profile answers the same questions, with sources. There is no score.

items.text: Is the faith central, or only the setting?
Does the film's own outlook fit traditional teaching? A character's errors are not the film's.
How does it treat Our Lord, Our Lady, the saints, the sacraments, priests and religious? Humour and flawed priests are not irreverent in themselves.
What is documented and what is invented, and do the inventions change the religious meaning?
What is good about the acting, images, writing, editing or music? Reputation alone does not count.
Does it reduce the supernatural to psychology, treat all religions as interchangeable, or recast doctrine? This has to be shown from the film, not assumed from who made it or when.
Is there a documented dispute about its religion or history? If so, it is described fairly.
Who is it for? Violence, sexual content and frightening scenes are noted separately, and a film that suits adults is not assumed to suit children.
Which ages is it suitable for, and why? Each page gives an age band (All ages, 8+, 12+, 15+ or Adults) with the reasons a parent would want to know.

sections.heading: Recommended, grey area or on hold
sections.text: A film that qualifies ends up in one of three places. Putting a film in the grey area or on hold does not mean nobody should watch it, and nothing here is a list of forbidden films.

items.text: The faith is central, the treatment meets the standard above, and independent sources support that. These are the films in the main list.

The film has real merit, but there is a definite doctrinal, moral or historical question about it, such as a Legion of Decency reservation or an invented episode that changes the religious meaning. Its page states the question so you can judge.
The film looks sound, but no independent review of how it treats the faith or the history has been found. Its page says what is known and where that comes from.
There is not yet enough reliable information to say what the film is or how it handles the faith. It is not listed until there is.

sections.after: New evidence can move a film either way. A grey-area film can become a recommendation, and any recommendation can be withdrawn.

sections.heading: Reference texts
sections.text: These Church documents shape the standard. They say nothing about individual films.

sections.heading: How judgments are made
sections.text: Profiles are written from published criticism, histories and biographies, archive and production records, and the films' release details. They do not claim that every film, or every cut of every film, has been watched for this site. Each profile lists its sources and what each one supports, and where critics disagree it says who thinks what.

sections.heading: Who decides
sections.text: The editor has the final say on what is included. Corrections and suggestions are always welcome.

about.title: About
about.lead: An independent guide to films about the Catholic faith.

sections.heading: What this is
sections.text: A selective guide to feature films, documentaries and television about the Catholic faith, from the silent era to the present. Each film has a page that says what it is, what it does well, what it invents, how it treats the faith and what to know before watching, with the sources used.

sections.heading: Who it is for
sections.text: Catholics looking for something worth watching; parents choosing films for their children; teachers and parish groups planning a screening; and anyone curious about how cinema has treated the Church.

sections.heading: The point of view
sections.text: Films are judged from a traditional Catholic standpoint. The site does not accept the Second Vatican Council or its reforms, and judges films by the Church's teaching as it stood before the Council. How that works in practice is set out on a separate page.

sections.heading: What it isn't
sections.text:
It is not an official publication of the Church, a diocese or a religious order, and it has no connection with any studio or distributor.

It is not complete. Many good films have not been researched yet, and some national cinemas are thinly covered. A missing film is more likely to be unresearched than rejected.

sections.heading: No ads, no tracking
sections.text: There is no advertising, no affiliate links, no sign-up and no tracking. The site is a set of static pages. The research behind it and the full catalogue data are public.

sources.title: Sources and research
sources.lead: Where the information on each film page comes from, and how much ground the research has covered.

sections.heading: Different questions, different sources
sections.text: Film institutes, archives and catalogues such as the BFI and the AFI Catalog establish the basic facts: title, year, director, country. Detailed reviews and essays show how a film treats its subject and how good it is. Histories and biographies show what actually happened. Church documents are the reference for doctrine. No single source answers all four questions.

sections.heading: Reading a film's sources
sections.text: Each film page ends with a numbered list of sources. Every entry gives the publisher, the date it was consulted and the specific points it supports. Sources with an interest in the film, such as its distributor or a religious order that helped make it, are identified as such. Links break, so the title and publisher are always recorded as well.

sections.heading: What the research does not claim
sections.text: It does not claim to cover every country, to have viewed every film or every cut, or to settle every disagreement between critics. Availability changes: a retailer listing found during research is not a promise that a film can be bought where you live.

corrections.title: Corrections
corrections.lead: Found a mistake, or know a film that should be here? Please say so.

sections.heading: Reporting a mistake
sections.text: Say which film and which statement is wrong, what it should say, and give a reliable source. If the problem only affects one version of the film, give the edition, language and running time.

sections.heading: Suggesting a film
sections.text: Give the original title, any English title, the year, the director and a source that identifies the film. Then explain why the Catholic faith is central to it, ideally with a review or essay that discusses how it handles the subject. A suggestion starts research; films are not added automatically.

sections.heading: Images and rights
sections.text: If you hold the rights to a poster or cover shown here and want it removed or credited differently, open an issue using the “Image or rights request” form. Images are removed promptly.

sections.heading: How reports are handled
sections.text:
Reports go through GitHub Issues, which needs a free GitHub account. Issues are public, so please leave out personal details, and don't post links to pirated copies or paste copyrighted text.

Factual changes need a source. If a report raises a serious problem with a recommended film, the film may be taken down while it is checked. Every change is kept in the site's version history.
